title: The 5 Reading Questions
subtitle: Every reading question is secretly one of five. Learn the five, and you always know what to look for.
quick_ref: Before answering, name which of the 5 it asks: What is it saying? · How do I prove it? · What is suggested? · How does it feel? · How is it built?
mini_lesson:
**Every reading question is one of five.**

A reading test can ask hundreds of different things. But underneath, almost every question is really asking one of just five questions. Learn to spot which one, and you always know what to look for — and which color to mark.

| The 5 questions | What the test actually asks | Mark it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What is the text really saying? | "What is the central idea or theme?" "What is the author's claim?" | Theme — blue |
| How do I prove it? | "Which detail best supports...?" "What evidence shows...?" | Evidence — green |
| What is suggested but not said? | "What can you infer?" "What does this imply?" | Inference — purple |
| How does the author feel, or make me feel? | "What is the tone?" "Why this word?" "What mood is created?" | Tone — amber |
| How is the text built? | "Why paragraph 3?" "How is this organized?" "What does this metaphor do?" | Structure — orange |

**Why these five.**

They are not random. They are the five moves an advanced reader makes on every hard text:

- **Saying** — find the point. (Theme, Main Idea, Topic, Claim)
- **Proving** — back it with exact text. (Evidence, Reasoning)
- **Suggesting** — read between the lines. (Inference, Point of View, Speaker)
- **Feeling** — catch the attitude and the mood. (Tone, Mood, Word Choice, Connotation, Purpose)
- **Building** — see how the parts fit. (Structure, Paragraph Function, Shift, Figurative Language)

**The five colors you will see everywhere.**

These same five are the five highlight colors in the Reading Lab and the Reading Library. When you mark up a real text, you are sorting it into these five. When you answer a question, you are picking which one it tests. Same five, every time.

**The first move on every question.**

Before you even read the answer choices, ask one thing: *which of the five is this question?* Naming it tells you exactly what to hunt for — and stops you from grabbing an answer that sounds smart but proves nothing.

> This question is really asking me: ______ (one of the five).

**How this connects to the rest.**

The next lesson (0.2) lays out the three MAP Reading areas and the specific tools inside each. This lesson is the lens; that one is the toolbox. After Module 0, every sub-concept drills one tool until it becomes automatic.
why_it_matters: At MAP 250+, the hardest skill is knowing what a question is really testing. Sorting every question into one of five makes the test legible — and it is the exact 5-color system you use to mark real texts.
